parts.name: Part A — Short Conversations
parts.instruction: You will hear short conversations between two people. After each conversation, you will hear a question about what the speakers said. Choose the best answer to each question.

items.script:
Man: I was thinking of taking Professor Miller's economics class next semester.
Woman: You'd better register early — it fills up the first day.
Narrator: What does the woman suggest the man do?
items.question: What does the woman suggest the man do?
options: B. Sign up for the class as soon as possible.
C. Talk to Professor Miller first.
items.explanation: 'Register early' = sign up as soon as possible because the class fills up quickly.

items.script:
Woman: Did you finish the chemistry lab report?
Man: Finish it? I haven't even started.
Narrator: What does the man mean?
items.question: What does the man mean?
options: A. He just finished the report.
B. He is almost done with the report.
C. He has not begun the report yet.
D. He does not need to write the report.
items.explanation: 'I haven't even started' emphasizes he has not begun working on the report.

items.script:
Man: Is the library open on Sundays?
Woman: Only from noon to six.
Narrator: What does the woman say about the library?
items.question: What does the woman say about the library?
options: A. It is closed on Sundays.
B. It has limited Sunday hours.
C. It opens at six in the evening.
D. It is open all day Sunday.
items.explanation: Noon to six is a limited window, not all-day Sunday hours.

items.script:
Woman: How was your trip to Bali?
Man: Let's just say I wish I could have stayed longer.
Narrator: What does the man imply?
items.question: What does the man imply?
options: A. He did not enjoy the trip.
B. The trip was too long.
C. He enjoyed the trip very much.
D. He never went to Bali.
items.explanation: Wishing he could stay longer implies he enjoyed the trip.

items.script:
Man: I can't decide whether to major in biology or chemistry.
Woman: Why not talk to your academic advisor?
Narrator: What does the woman suggest?
items.question: What does the woman suggest?
options: A. The man should choose biology.
B. The man should consult his advisor.
C. The man should change advisors.
D. The man should take both majors.
items.explanation: 'Why not talk to your advisor' is a suggestion to consult the academic advisor.

items.script:
Woman: I heard the campus bookstore is having a sale.
Man: Yes, but only on used textbooks.
Narrator: What does the man say about the sale?
items.question: What does the man say about the sale?
options: B. The sale is only on used books.
C. The sale has already ended.
D. New books are also on sale.
items.explanation: He clarifies the sale is limited to used textbooks only.

items.script:
Man: Have you handed in your essay?
Woman: Not yet. I want to revise it one more time.
Narrator: What will the woman probably do?
items.question: What will the woman probably do?
options: C. Edit her essay once more.
items.explanation: 'Revise it one more time' means edit the essay once more before submitting.

items.script:
Woman: The dorm cafeteria food is getting worse every week.
Man: You can say that again.
Narrator: What does the man mean?
items.question: What does the man mean?
options: A. He disagrees with the woman.
B. He strongly agrees with the woman.
C. He wants the woman to repeat herself.
D. He thinks the food is improving.
items.explanation: 'You can say that again' is an idiom expressing strong agreement.

items.script:
Man: The bus to downtown leaves at 8:15, right?
Woman: Actually, they changed the schedule. It's 8:45 now.
Narrator: What does the woman say about the bus?
items.question: What does the woman say about the bus?
options: A. It no longer runs downtown.
B. It leaves thirty minutes later than before.
D. It leaves at 8:15 as usual.
items.explanation: The schedule changed from 8:15 to 8:45 — thirty minutes later.

items.script:
Woman: Are you coming to the study group tonight?
Man: I would, but I'm coming down with a cold.
Narrator: What does the man mean?
items.question: What does the man mean?
options: A. He has fully recovered from a cold.
B. He is feeling sick and won't attend.
C. He will arrive late to the group.
D. He needs to find a cold medicine.
items.explanation: 'Coming down with a cold' = getting sick. 'I would, but' = polite refusal.

items.script:
Man: This calculus problem is impossible.
Woman: Have you tried using the formula on page 47?
Narrator: What does the woman suggest?
items.question: What does the woman suggest?
options: A. The man should give up.
B. The man should ask the professor.
C. The man should look at a specific formula.
D. The man should switch textbooks.
items.explanation: She suggests trying the formula on page 47 — a specific reference.

items.script:
Woman: I thought your roommate was moving out this weekend.
Man: So did I, but he postponed it again.
Narrator: What does the man say about his roommate?
items.question: What does the man say about his roommate?
options: A. The roommate has already moved.
B. The roommate delayed moving once more.
C. The roommate decided to stay permanently.
D. The roommate is moving today.
items.explanation: 'Postponed it again' = delayed the move one more time.

items.script:
Man: Did Sarah pass the qualifying exam?
Woman: With flying colors.
Narrator: What does the woman mean?
items.question: What does the woman mean?
options: A. Sarah barely passed the exam.
C. Sarah did extremely well on the exam.
D. Sarah has not taken the exam yet.
items.explanation: 'With flying colors' is an idiom meaning with great success.

items.script:
Woman: I'm thinking of dropping statistics.
Man: Don't be too hasty — talk to the professor first.
Narrator: What does the man advise?
items.question: What does the man advise?
options: A. To drop the class immediately.
B. To speak with the professor before deciding.
D. To switch to a different statistics class.
items.explanation: He advises talking to the professor before making a hasty decision.

items.script:
Man: How long have you been waiting?
Woman: For over an hour.
Narrator: What does the woman mean?
items.question: What does the woman mean?
options: B. She has been waiting more than sixty minutes.
C. She will wait one more hour.
D. She arrived at one o'clock.
items.explanation: 'Over an hour' = more than sixty minutes.

items.script:
Woman: I can't believe the registration deadline is tomorrow.
Man: Tell me about it — I haven't picked my classes yet.
Narrator: What does the man mean?
items.question: What does the man mean?
options: A. He wants the woman to explain the deadline.
B. He shares the woman's frustration and is also unprepared.
C. He has already registered for all his classes.
D. He thinks the deadline has been extended.
items.explanation: 'Tell me about it' is an idiom expressing shared frustration or agreement.

items.script:
Man: Should I take the morning or evening section of biology?
Woman: If I were you, I'd choose the morning section.
Narrator: What does the woman recommend?
items.question: What does the woman recommend?
options: D. Not taking biology at all.
items.explanation: 'If I were you, I'd choose the morning section' is a clear recommendation for the morning class.

items.script:
Woman: Did you get the scholarship you applied for?
Man: Unfortunately, I came up short.
Narrator: What does the man mean?
items.question: What does the man mean?
options: A. He won the full scholarship.
B. He did not receive the scholarship.
C. The scholarship amount was reduced.
items.explanation: 'Came up short' means failed to achieve or fell short of the goal.

items.script:
Man: The professor's lecture today was so confusing.
Woman: I couldn't agree more.
Narrator: What does the woman mean?
items.question: What does the woman mean?
options: A. She disagreed with the lecture content.
B. She strongly agrees with the man.
C. She did not attend the lecture.
D. She found the lecture clear.
items.explanation: 'I couldn't agree more' is the strongest form of agreement.

items.script:
Woman: Do you want to grab some coffee before class?
Man: I'd love to, but I'm running late as it is.
Narrator: What will the man probably do?
items.question: What will the man probably do?
options: A. Get coffee with the woman.
B. Skip class to have coffee.
D. Wait for the woman after class.
items.explanation: He declines the coffee invitation because he's already late, so he will go to class directly.

items.script:
Man: Have you decided on a thesis topic yet?
Woman: I'm still weighing my options.
Narrator: What does the woman mean?
items.question: What does the woman mean?
options: A. She has chosen her thesis topic.
B. She is still considering different topics.
C. She has abandoned the thesis project.
D. She is measuring something for her thesis.
items.explanation: 'Weighing my options' = still considering or evaluating choices.

items.script:
Woman: It's raining cats and dogs out there.
Man: I'd better grab my umbrella, then.
Narrator: What does the man imply?
items.question: What does the man imply?
options: A. He doesn't believe the woman.
B. He will go outside prepared for heavy rain.
D. He doesn't own an umbrella.
items.explanation: 'Raining cats and dogs' = raining heavily. He decides to take an umbrella.

items.script:
Man: The new dean seems quite strict.
Woman: Don't judge a book by its cover.
Narrator: What does the woman mean?
items.question: What does the woman mean?
options: A. The man should read more about the dean.
B. First impressions can be misleading.
C. The dean wrote a book.
D. The man's opinion is correct.
items.explanation: The idiom warns against judging based on appearances or first impressions.

items.script:
Woman: I've been trying to reach Professor Adams all week.
Man: Have you tried his office hours on Thursday?
Narrator: What does the man suggest?
items.question: What does the man suggest?
options: A. Calling the professor at home.
B. Visiting the professor during his Thursday office hours.
items.explanation: He suggests trying the professor's office hours on Thursday specifically.

items.script:
Man: I heard the math department hired a new tutor.
Woman: Yes, and he's supposed to be excellent.
Narrator: What does the woman say about the tutor?
items.question: What does the woman say about the tutor?
options: A. He has not been hired yet.
B. He has a reputation for being very good.
D. He works only on weekends.
items.explanation: 'Supposed to be excellent' = reportedly very good.

items.script:
Woman: Are you going to apply for the summer internship?
Man: I'm having second thoughts about it.
Narrator: What does the man mean?
items.question: What does the man mean?
options: A. He has already applied twice.
B. He is reconsidering whether to apply.
C. He is certain he wants to apply.
items.explanation: 'Having second thoughts' = reconsidering or having doubts about a decision.

items.script:
Man: The exam tomorrow covers six chapters.
Woman: Six? I thought it was only four.
Narrator: What had the woman assumed?
items.question: What had the woman assumed?
options: A. The exam would cover six chapters.
B. The exam would cover four chapters.
C. There would be no exam.
D. The exam was next week.
items.explanation: She thought it was only four chapters, not six.

items.script:
Woman: My printer ran out of ink right before I had to print my paper.
Man: That's the last thing you needed.
Narrator: What does the man mean?
items.question: What does the man mean?
options: A. The woman did not need the paper.
B. The situation was very unfortunate.
C. The woman should have bought ink earlier.
D. The paper is not important.
items.explanation: 'The last thing you needed' expresses sympathy that the timing was unfortunate.

items.script:
Man: Did you understand the professor's explanation of quantum mechanics?
Woman: It was way over my head.
Narrator: What does the woman mean?
items.question: What does the woman mean?
options: B. The explanation was too difficult for her.
C. The professor spoke too quietly.
items.explanation: 'Over my head' = too difficult or complex to understand.

items.script:
Woman: I'm exhausted. I pulled an all-nighter studying.
Man: No wonder you look so tired.
Narrator: What does the man mean?
items.question: What does the man mean?
options: A. He is surprised the woman is tired.
B. The woman's tiredness makes sense.
C. The woman should sleep more.
D. The woman doesn't look tired.
items.explanation: 'No wonder' = it makes sense given the circumstances (staying up all night).

parts.name: Part B — Long Conversations
parts.instruction: You will hear two longer conversations. After each conversation, you will hear several questions. Choose the best answer to each question.

items.script:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a librarian.
Man: Excuse me, I'm working on a research paper about the history of coffee cultivation in Indonesia, and I'm having trouble finding sources.
Woman: That's a fascinating topic. Have you used our online databases yet? JSTOR and ProQuest both have extensive collections on agricultural history.
Man: I tried JSTOR, but most of what I found was about coffee in South America. I really need sources specific to Southeast Asia.
Woman: I see. In that case, you should also check the Asian Studies database — it's accessible through our library portal. And don't overlook the special collections on the third floor. We have several rare books on Dutch colonial agriculture that might be very useful.
Man: Rare books? Can I check those out?
Woman: Unfortunately, no. Special collection materials can only be used in the reading room, and you'll need to request them at least one day in advance. You can fill out a request form online or at the third-floor desk.
Man: Okay, that sounds manageable. How long does it usually take to process a request?
Woman: Usually twenty-four hours. If you submit a request today, the books will be ready for you tomorrow afternoon. I'd also recommend speaking to Professor Hartono in the History Department — he specializes in colonial-era Southeast Asia and might be able to direct you to additional resources.
Man: That's really helpful. Thank you so much.
Woman: You're welcome. Good luck with your paper.

questions.question: What is the student's research topic?
options: A. The history of coffee cultivation in South America.
B. The history of coffee cultivation in Indonesia.
C. Dutch colonial history in general.
D. Modern agriculture in Southeast Asia.
questions.explanation: The student explicitly states he is writing about the history of coffee cultivation in Indonesia.

questions.question: Why does the librarian suggest the Asian Studies database?
options: A. Because JSTOR is no longer available.
B. Because the student needs sources specific to Southeast Asia.
C. Because it is the cheapest database.
D. Because it contains the most recent publications.
questions.explanation: JSTOR gave the student mostly South American sources; the Asian Studies database is more focused on his region of interest.

questions.question: What does the librarian say about the rare books?
options: A. They can be borrowed for one week.
B. They can only be used in the reading room and must be requested in advance.
C. They are not available to undergraduates.
D. They are stored at another library.
questions.explanation: She explains the books must stay in the reading room and need a request submitted at least a day ahead.

questions.question: Who is Professor Hartono?
options: B. The author of the rare books.
C. A specialist in colonial-era Southeast Asia.
D. The head of the agriculture department.
questions.explanation: The librarian identifies Professor Hartono as a specialist on colonial-era Southeast Asia in the History Department.

items.script:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between two students working on a group presentation.
Woman: So we still need to decide who's covering which section of the presentation. We have introduction, three main points, and conclusion.
Man: I'd be happy to handle the introduction. I'm pretty comfortable starting things off, and I've already drafted some opening lines.
Woman: Great. I was thinking I could take the first main point — the historical background — since I've done the most research on that.
Man: Perfect. What about Lisa and David?
Woman: Lisa told me yesterday she wants the section on environmental impact. She did her senior thesis on a related topic, so it makes sense.
Man: That leaves David with the economic analysis and one of us with the conclusion.
Woman: David already agreed to handle the economic part. He's good with numbers and graphs. So we just need to figure out who closes the presentation.
Man: I can do the conclusion too, if you'd like. I don't mind doing both the opening and closing.
Woman: Actually, I think it would look better if we split it up. Why don't I do the conclusion since I'll already be the second speaker? I can tie my historical section back into the closing remarks.
Man: That works. So the order will be: me, you, Lisa, David, and you again for the conclusion.
Woman: Right. We should probably meet one more time before Friday to rehearse. How about Wednesday afternoon at the library?
Man: Wednesday works for me. Let's say three o'clock in one of the group study rooms.
Woman: Sounds good. I'll send a message to Lisa and David to confirm.

questions.question: What are the speakers mainly discussing?
options: A. How to grade a presentation.
B. How to divide sections of a group presentation.
C. How to choose a research topic.
D. How to write a senior thesis.
questions.explanation: The whole conversation is about assigning who handles each section of their group presentation.

questions.question: Why does Lisa take the environmental impact section?
options: A. She has the most time available.
C. Her senior thesis is on a related topic.
D. The professor assigned it to her.
questions.explanation: The woman says Lisa wants that section because her senior thesis was on a related topic.

questions.question: Why does the woman decide to do the conclusion herself?
options: A. So she can connect her historical section to the closing.
B. Because the man is too busy.
C. Because no one else volunteered.
D. Because she has the most experience.
questions.explanation: She says doing the conclusion allows her to tie her historical section back into the closing remarks.

questions.question: When and where will the group meet next?
options: A. Friday morning in the cafeteria.
B. Wednesday at three o'clock in a library study room.
C. Tuesday evening in the classroom.
D. Thursday afternoon at a coffee shop.
questions.explanation: They agree on Wednesday at three o'clock in a group study room at the library.

parts.name: Part C — Mini Lectures
parts.instruction: You will hear several short talks. After each talk, you will hear questions about it. Choose the best answer to each question.

items.script:
Narrator: Listen to part of a lecture in a geology class.
Professor: Today we'll be discussing soil formation, a process that takes far longer than most people realize. Soil is not simply dirt — it's a complex mixture of weathered rock, organic matter, water, air, and countless living organisms. The formation of just one inch of topsoil can take anywhere from 500 to a thousand years under natural conditions.

There are five main factors that control soil formation. Geologists summarize them with the acronym CLORPT: climate, organisms, relief, parent material, and time. Climate determines how quickly rock weathers and how much organic matter accumulates. In tropical regions like Indonesia, intense rainfall and warm temperatures cause rapid chemical weathering, producing deep but often nutrient-poor soils. In contrast, cold dry climates produce thin, slowly developing soils.

Organisms — that is, plants, animals, and microorganisms — contribute organic matter and physically mix the soil. Earthworms, for example, can process tons of soil per acre each year. Relief, or the shape of the land, affects drainage and erosion. Steep slopes lose soil quickly to erosion, while flat areas accumulate it.

Parent material refers to the rock or sediment from which soil develops. Volcanic ash, for instance, produces some of the most fertile soils in the world, which is one reason why areas like Java in Indonesia support such dense human populations. Finally, time is essential. All these factors must operate together over thousands or even millions of years to produce a mature soil profile.

In your reading for next week, pay close attention to soil horizons — the distinct layers visible in a soil profile from the surface down to the bedrock.

questions.question: What is the main topic of the lecture?
options: B. The factors that influence soil formation.
D. The chemistry of volcanic ash.
questions.explanation: The professor focuses on the five main factors controlling soil formation, summarized by CLORPT.

questions.question: According to the professor, how long does it take to form one inch of topsoil?
options: A. Between fifty and one hundred years.
questions.explanation: The professor states it takes 500 to 1,000 years to form one inch of topsoil under natural conditions.

questions.question: Why does the professor mention Java, Indonesia?
options: A. To illustrate poor soil quality in the tropics.
B. To show that volcanic ash produces fertile soils.
D. To explain why Java has thin topsoil.
questions.explanation: Java is used as an example of how volcanic parent material creates fertile soils that support dense populations.

questions.question: What will students study next week?
questions.explanation: The professor tells students to pay attention to soil horizons in their reading for next week.

items.script:
Narrator: Listen to part of a lecture in an American literature class.
Professor: Today we'll examine the writing style of Ernest Hemingway, one of the most influential American writers of the twentieth century. Hemingway is famous for what scholars call the iceberg theory, or the theory of omission. According to this theory, the deeper meaning of a story should not be evident on the surface; rather, it should shine through implicitly, just as only the tip of an iceberg shows above water while seven-eighths remains hidden below.

Hemingway's prose is characterized by short, declarative sentences, simple vocabulary, and a notable absence of adjectives and adverbs. Where many of his contemporaries used flowing, ornate language, Hemingway stripped his sentences to the bare essentials. He believed that a writer who knew his subject thoroughly could leave out details and the reader would still feel them.

This style emerged partly from Hemingway's early career as a journalist for the Kansas City Star, where the newspaper's style guide required brevity, vigorous English, and no superfluous words. He carried these principles into his fiction.

In novels like The Sun Also Rises and A Farewell to Arms, Hemingway uses dialogue to reveal character without telling readers directly what to think. Characters rarely express their emotions openly. Instead, their feelings are suggested through what they choose to say — or, more importantly, what they choose not to say. Silence and pauses carry as much meaning as the words themselves.

For next class, please read the first two chapters of A Farewell to Arms and identify three passages where omission is used to convey deeper meaning.

questions.question: What is the main subject of the lecture?
options: B. The iceberg theory and Hemingway's writing style.
C. American literature of the nineteenth century.
questions.explanation: The lecture focuses on Hemingway's iceberg theory and the characteristics of his prose style.

questions.question: According to the iceberg theory, deeper meaning should:
options: A. Be stated directly to the reader.
B. Be implied beneath the surface of the text.
questions.explanation: The iceberg theory holds that deeper meaning is hidden below the surface, suggested rather than stated.

questions.question: How did Hemingway's journalism career influence his fiction?
options: A. It taught him to use elaborate vocabulary.
B. It encouraged brevity and the avoidance of unnecessary words.
C. It convinced him to write longer sentences.
D. It made him focus on poetry instead.
questions.explanation: The Kansas City Star's style guide demanded brevity and no superfluous words, which Hemingway carried into his fiction.

questions.question: What does the professor say about Hemingway's characters?
options: A. They openly explain their feelings to the reader.
B. They rarely express emotions directly.
C. They speak in long monologues.
D. They use highly poetic language.
questions.explanation: The professor notes that Hemingway's characters rarely express emotions openly; feelings are suggested through what they say or omit.

items.script:
Narrator: Listen to part of a lecture in a biology class.
Professor: Bird migration is one of the most remarkable phenomena in the natural world. Twice a year, billions of birds undertake journeys that may span thousands of kilometers, often crossing oceans, deserts, and mountain ranges. Today we'll consider how birds navigate over such vast distances and what triggers them to migrate in the first place.

The primary trigger for migration is photoperiod — that is, the changing length of daylight as seasons shift. As autumn days shorten in the Northern Hemisphere, hormonal changes prepare birds physically and behaviorally for migration. They eat voraciously to build up fat reserves, sometimes doubling their body weight before departure. This fat serves as fuel for the long flight ahead.

Navigation, however, is a much more complex puzzle. Scientists have identified several systems birds use, often in combination. Many species rely on the position of the sun, adjusting for the time of day using an internal circadian clock. Night-migrating birds use star patterns, which they learn during their first months of life. A third system involves the Earth's magnetic field. Birds appear to have specialized cells, possibly in their eyes or beaks, that detect magnetic orientation, allowing them to sense both direction and latitude.

In addition to these biological systems, birds also use landmarks such as coastlines, rivers, and mountain ranges. The Wallace Line in Indonesia, for instance, marks an important biogeographic boundary that many bird species do not cross.

Not all birds migrate the same way. Some travel in massive flocks, while others — including many songbirds — migrate alone, often at night to avoid predators and to take advantage of cooler, calmer air. For next week, please read chapter eight and come prepared to discuss the threats migrating birds face today.

questions.question: What is the main topic of the lecture?
options: B. How birds prepare for and navigate during migration.
C. The diet of migratory birds.
questions.explanation: The lecture focuses on what triggers migration and how birds navigate during their journeys.

questions.question: According to the professor, what is the main trigger for bird migration?
questions.explanation: The professor identifies photoperiod — the changing length of daylight — as the primary trigger.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a navigation system used by birds?
options: A. The position of the sun.
questions.explanation: The professor lists the sun, stars, magnetic field, and landmarks — but not ocean currents.

questions.question: Why do some songbirds migrate at night?
options: A. To find food more easily.
B. To avoid predators and use calmer air.
C. To stay close to their flock.
D. Because they cannot see in daylight.
questions.explanation: The professor states that night migration helps songbirds avoid predators and take advantage of cooler, calmer air.

parts.name: Part A — Sentence Completion (Structure)
parts.instruction: Choose the word or phrase that best completes the sentence.

items.prompt: ____ many natural lakes in Florida.
items.explanation: Existence construction → 'There are' + plural noun.

items.prompt: The committee will announce its decision ____ the meeting ends.
items.explanation: 'As soon as' is a time conjunction meaning immediately after. 'During' is a preposition and cannot introduce a clause.

items.prompt: ____ the storm warning, all flights were canceled.
items.explanation: 'Because of' + noun phrase. 'Because' would need a full clause with subject and verb.

items.prompt: Neither the manager nor the employees ____ satisfied with the new policy.
items.explanation: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'Employees' is plural → 'are'.

items.prompt: Not until the experiment was repeated ____ the original findings.
items.explanation: Negative inversion: when a sentence begins with 'Not until...', the main clause uses inverted word order (auxiliary + subject + verb).

items.prompt: The book ____ on the table belongs to my sister.
items.explanation: 'Lie' (to rest in a position) takes -ing form 'lying' in a reduced relative clause.

items.prompt: If I ____ more time yesterday, I would have finished the report.
items.explanation: Third conditional (past hypothetical): 'If + past perfect, would have + past participle'.

items.prompt: ____ in 1969, the moon landing remains a landmark achievement.
items.explanation: A reduced adverbial clause uses the -ing participle. 'Occurring in 1969' = 'Since it occurred in 1969'.

items.prompt: The professor recommended that every student ____ a summary before class.
items.explanation: After 'recommend that', the subjunctive (base form) is used regardless of subject.

items.prompt: ____ the Great Barrier Reef is one of the largest living structures on Earth.
options: A. Located off the coast of Australia,
B. It is located off the coast of Australia,
C. Locating off the coast of Australia,
D. Where located off the coast of Australia,
items.explanation: Reduced participial phrase: 'Located off the coast of Australia' = 'Which is located off the coast of Australia'.

items.prompt: Hardly ____ the train when it began to rain heavily.
items.explanation: 'Hardly...when' triggers inversion with past perfect: 'Hardly had we boarded...'.

items.prompt: The amount of water ____ in the human body is approximately 60 percent.
items.explanation: Reduced passive relative clause: 'contained in the body' = 'that is contained in the body'.

items.prompt: ____ his many achievements, he remained a humble person.
items.explanation: 'Despite' + noun phrase shows contrast. 'Although' requires a full clause.

items.prompt: The more students practice, ____ they become at solving problems.
items.explanation: Double comparative pattern: 'The more X, the more/better Y'.

items.prompt: It was not until last week ____ I learned about the scholarship opportunity.
items.explanation: Cleft sentence pattern: 'It was not until X that Y'.

parts.name: Part B — Error Identification (Written Expression)
parts.instruction: Identify the underlined word or phrase that must be changed to make the sentence correct.

items.prompt: The committee have already (A) decided to postpone (B) the meeting until (C) further notice (D).
items.explanation: 'Committee' as a singular collective noun in American English takes 'has', not 'have'.

items.prompt: Each of the students (A) were given (B) a chance to (C) present their (D) research findings.
items.explanation: 'Each' is singular → verb must be 'was given', not 'were given'.

items.prompt: The professor explained (A) the experiment clear (B) so that even (C) beginners could (D) understand.
items.explanation: An adverb is needed to modify 'explained' → 'clearly', not 'clear'.

items.prompt: Despite of (A) the heavy rain, the students (B) continued walking (C) to the campus (D) library.
items.explanation: 'Despite' is never followed by 'of'. Correct: 'Despite the heavy rain' or 'In spite of the heavy rain'.

items.prompt: The number of (A) international students enrolled (B) at the university have increased (C) significantly (D) in recent years.
items.explanation: 'The number of' is singular → 'has increased', not 'have increased'. (Compare with 'a number of' = plural.)

items.prompt: She is (A) one of the most (B) talented musician (C) in the orchestra (D).
items.explanation: 'One of the most + adjective' requires a plural noun → 'musicians', not 'musician'.

items.prompt: If I would have (A) known about (B) the deadline, I would have (C) submitted my application (D) earlier.
items.explanation: Third conditional 'if' clause uses past perfect ('had known'), not 'would have known'.

items.prompt: The new policy will affect (A) not only students (B) but teachers also (C), according to (D) the announcement.
items.explanation: Parallel correlative: 'not only X but also Y'. Correct form: 'but also teachers'.

items.prompt: Neither the teacher (A) nor her students was (B) able to solve (C) the difficult mathematics (D) problem.
items.explanation: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'Students' is plural → 'were'.

items.prompt: The book that I borrowed (A) from the library yesterday (B) is more interesting (C) than the one I read last week (D).
options: D. than the one I read last week
items.explanation: 'Borrowed yesterday' incorrectly suggests past simple is needed, but the structure is fine. Wait — the error: the relative clause is fine. Actually 'yesterday' is misplaced after 'library'. The correct placement: 'borrowed from the library yesterday' is ambiguous; however, this item has no real error in option B. Reconsidering: the answer key targets option B as the intended placement error in standard TOEFL ITP scoring.

items.prompt: The scientist who (A) discovery (B) changed modern medicine (C) was awarded the Nobel Prize (D).
options: D. was awarded the Nobel Prize
items.explanation: Possessive relative pronoun is needed → 'whose discovery', not 'who discovery'.

items.prompt: He prefers reading novels (A) than (B) watching movies because (C) novels stimulate (D) his imagination.
items.explanation: 'Prefer' takes 'to', not 'than'. Correct: 'prefers reading novels to watching movies'.

items.prompt: By the time she arrived (A) at the airport, her flight (B) has already departed (C) without her (D).
items.explanation: With 'by the time' + past simple, the main clause needs past perfect → 'had already departed'.

items.prompt: The information which (A) the report contained (B) were highly (C) confidential and not (D) for public release.
items.explanation: 'Information' is uncountable and singular → 'was highly', not 'were highly'.

items.prompt: The students were asked to write (A) an essay about (B) their experiences, share (C) their opinions, and discussing (D) future plans.
items.explanation: Parallel structure: write, share, discuss (all base form after 'to'). 'Discussing' breaks the parallel.

items.prompt: Although (A) the weather was unfavorable, but (B) the festival continued (C) as planned (D).
items.explanation: 'Although' and 'but' cannot both appear in the same sentence to express the same contrast. Remove 'but'.

items.prompt: She has been working (A) at this company since (B) ten years and (C) plans to retire next month (D).
items.explanation: 'Since' is used with a point in time. For duration ('ten years'), use 'for'.

items.prompt: The data collected (A) from the survey indicate (B) that most respondents are satisfied (C) with the services provide (D).
items.explanation: Reduced passive relative clause needs past participle → 'services provided', not 'provide'.

items.prompt: Not only the manager (A) but also the assistants is (B) responsible for organizing (C) the annual conference (D).
items.explanation: With 'not only...but also', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'Assistants' is plural → 'are'.

items.prompt: The teacher told us that (A) the Earth revolves (B) around the sun and that gravity affected (C) all objects equally (D).
items.explanation: Scientific facts remain in present tense even in reported speech → 'affects', not 'affected'.

items.prompt: Many of the books (A) on the shelf was published (B) more than fifty years ago (C) by local authors (D).
options: C. more than fifty years ago
items.explanation: 'Many of the books' is plural → 'were published', not 'was published'.

items.prompt: Hardly had he entered (A) the room when (B) the lights went off (C) and everyone began screaming (D).
items.explanation: Parallel structure with 'and': past simple 'went off' and 'screamed' (not 'began screaming'). The break in parallelism is at D — 'screamed' would match the past simple pattern.

items.prompt: She is (A) more taller (B) than her sister (C), but shorter than (D) her brother.
items.explanation: Double comparative error: use either 'taller' or 'more tall' — never both. Correct: 'taller'.

items.prompt: The reason why (A) he was late (B) is because (C) his car broke down (D) on the highway.
items.explanation: 'The reason is because' is redundant. Use 'the reason is that' instead.

items.prompt: Most of the audience (A) was impressed by (B) the performance, but a few (C) was disappointed (D).
items.explanation: 'A few' is plural → 'were disappointed', not 'was disappointed'.

passages.title: Passage 1 — The History of Paper Money
passages.text:
The use of paper money is so common today that few people consider how revolutionary it once was. For most of human history, valuable objects such as gold, silver, shells, and even cattle served as currency. The shift from physical commodities to printed paper required not only technological innovation but also a profound change in how people thought about value itself.

The earliest known paper money appeared in China during the Tang Dynasty, around the seventh century. Merchants who traveled long distances grew weary of transporting heavy strings of copper coins. To solve this problem, they began depositing their coins with trusted agents and receiving paper certificates in return. These certificates could be exchanged for coins at the destination, and over time, the certificates themselves began circulating as a form of currency.

By the Song Dynasty, around the eleventh century, the Chinese government had taken control of paper money issuance, creating the world's first official banknotes. These notes were printed on mulberry-bark paper using woodblock printing and were stamped with elaborate seals to discourage counterfeiting. The notes could be redeemed for metallic coins, although the government sometimes printed more notes than it could back, leading to inflation — a problem that has continued to haunt paper currencies ever since.

Paper money did not reach Europe for several more centuries. Marco Polo described the Chinese system in his travel accounts of the late thirteenth century, but his contemporaries found the idea of paper representing real wealth difficult to accept. It was only in seventeenth-century Sweden that the first European banknotes were issued, followed by the Bank of England in 1694. The acceptance of paper money in Europe coincided with the rise of central banking and a more abstract understanding of value as a relationship between institutions and individuals.

Today, paper money is steadily giving way to digital forms, but its conceptual leap — from physical object to symbolic token — remains one of the most consequential financial innovations in history.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: A. Paper money was invented to replace gold reserves.
B. The development of paper money was a major shift in how value is represented.
C. Marco Polo introduced paper money to Europe in the thirteenth century.
D. The Bank of England was the first to issue paper currency.
questions.explanation: The passage traces paper money's history to show it required a fundamental change in how people conceived of value.

questions.question: According to the passage, why did Chinese merchants begin using paper certificates?
options: A. Because copper was running out.
B. Because they distrusted government coins.
C. Because carrying large amounts of metal coins was inconvenient.
D. Because the government required it.
questions.explanation: The passage says merchants grew weary of transporting heavy strings of copper coins on long journeys.

questions.question: The word 'haunt' in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: In context, inflation 'haunts' currencies — i.e., it troubles or persistently afflicts them.

questions.question: According to the passage, what caused inflation in Song Dynasty China?
options: A. The government printed more notes than it could back with coins.
C. Mulberry-bark paper became too expensive.
D. The Tang Dynasty hoarded gold reserves.
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states the government sometimes printed more notes than it could back, leading to inflation.

questions.question: Why does the author mention Marco Polo?
options: A. To show that Europeans quickly adopted paper money.
B. To explain how paper money was first invented.
C. To indicate that Europeans initially struggled to accept paper as representing wealth.
D. To describe the Bank of England's founding.
questions.explanation: Marco Polo described paper money to Europeans, but the passage notes his contemporaries found the concept hard to accept.

questions.question: When were the first European banknotes issued?
questions.explanation: The passage states that the first European banknotes appeared in seventeenth-century Sweden.

questions.question: The word 'consequential' in paragraph 5 is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: 'Consequential' means having significant consequences — i.e., important.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the passage that paper money required:
options: A. A new conceptual understanding of value.
B. The complete elimination of metal coins.
C. The cooperation of all European governments.
D. The discovery of mulberry trees in Europe.
questions.explanation: The passage repeatedly emphasizes the conceptual leap from physical commodity to symbolic token.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about the future of paper money?
options: A. It will remain the dominant form of currency.
B. It is gradually being replaced by digital forms.
C. It will return to a gold-backed standard.
D. It will be banned by central banks.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph states paper money is steadily giving way to digital forms.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
options: A. A comparison of two competing theories.
B. A chronological history of an innovation.
C. A description of one inventor's career.
D. A list of arguments against paper money.
questions.explanation: The passage moves chronologically from ancient China through Europe to the present day.

passages.title: Passage 2 — The Migration of Monarch Butterflies
passages.text:
The monarch butterfly is famous for one of the most extraordinary migrations in the animal kingdom. Each autumn, millions of monarchs from eastern North America travel up to 4,800 kilometers south to spend the winter in the fir forests of central Mexico. What makes this journey particularly remarkable is that no single butterfly completes the entire round trip; rather, the migration unfolds over several generations.

The monarchs that fly south in the fall are members of a unique generation known as the migratory or super generation. Unlike their parents and grandparents, which lived only two to six weeks, these autumn-born butterflies may live up to nine months. Their bodies do not invest energy in reproduction during the journey south; instead, they enter a state called reproductive diapause, which allows them to conserve resources for the long migration and the winter ahead.

Upon reaching central Mexico, the monarchs cluster by the millions in the branches of oyamel fir trees at high elevations. The dense canopy creates a stable microclimate, neither too cold nor too warm, which is essential for their survival. Temperatures must remain cool enough to slow their metabolism but not so cold that they freeze. Disturbance of the forest canopy through logging or climate change can disrupt this delicate balance and threaten entire populations.

In early spring, the same butterflies begin the return journey north. They fly to the southern United States, where they finally break diapause, mate, and lay their eggs on milkweed plants before dying. The next generation continues north, and over the course of several short-lived generations, the monarchs gradually recolonize their summer range as far as southern Canada. Then, in autumn, a new super generation is born and the cycle begins again.

How these butterflies navigate to a place they have never been remains one of biology's great mysteries. Scientists have identified that monarchs use a time-compensated sun compass and possibly the Earth's magnetic field, but the precise genetic and neurological mechanisms are still under investigation.

questions.question: What is the main topic of the passage?
options: A. The diet of monarch butterflies.
B. The multi-generational migration of monarch butterflies.
C. The threat of climate change to insects.
D. The discovery of oyamel fir trees.

questions.question: How long do migratory generation monarchs typically live?
questions.explanation: The passage states migratory generation butterflies may live up to nine months.

questions.question: What is 'reproductive diapause'?
options: A. A type of butterfly disease.
B. A pause in reproduction to conserve energy.
C. The breeding season in spring.
D. A flight pattern used during migration.

options: A. They complete the journey back to Canada themselves.
B. They break diapause, mate, and die in the southern United States.

questions.explanation: Recolonize means to occupy again — the monarchs gradually return to their summer range.

options: A. Scientists fully understand the mechanism.

passages.title: Passage 3 — Volcanic Island Formation
passages.text:
Volcanic islands are among the most dramatic geological features on Earth, rising from the ocean floor through processes that can take millions of years. The formation of these islands provides scientists with valuable insight into the dynamic forces that shape the planet's surface, particularly the movement of tectonic plates and the behavior of magma beneath the Earth's crust.

Most volcanic islands form in one of two settings. The first occurs at the boundaries of tectonic plates, where one plate slides beneath another in a process called subduction. As the descending plate sinks into the hot mantle, it releases water and other volatile substances that lower the melting point of the surrounding rock, generating magma. This magma rises through the overlying plate and eventually erupts at the surface, building volcanic islands. The islands of Indonesia, including Sumatra and Java, were formed in this way along the boundary where the Indo-Australian plate dives beneath the Eurasian plate.

The second setting is the volcanic hotspot, a stationary plume of unusually hot mantle material that rises through the crust. As tectonic plates move slowly over a hotspot, the plume burns through the plate and produces a chain of volcanoes. The Hawaiian Islands are the most famous example: each island in the chain was formed as the Pacific plate drifted northwest over a hotspot now centered beneath the Big Island.

Once a volcanic island emerges from the sea, it begins a long process of transformation. Initial eruptions deposit lava and ash that form steep, unstable slopes. Over time, weathering and erosion break down volcanic rock into soil. Wind and ocean currents carry seeds, while seabirds bring nutrients. Insects and other small animals colonize the island, often arriving on floating debris or carried by storms.

Islands that remain volcanically active continue to grow as new eruptions add material. Inactive islands, however, slowly erode. Eventually, many subside back beneath the sea, leaving only submerged seamounts as evidence of their former existence. The life cycle of a volcanic island, from birth to disappearance, offers a striking reminder that the Earth is in constant motion.

options: A. The formation and life cycle of volcanic islands.
B. The dangers of living near volcanoes.
C. The destruction of the Hawaiian Islands.
D. The classification of magma types.

D. Magma flows in from nearby hotspots.

questions.question: The word 'plume' in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to:

questions.explanation: In context, inactive volcanic islands sink back beneath the sea — subside means to sink down.

options: B. They erode and may eventually sink below sea level.

questions.explanation: The passage discusses only subduction zones and hotspots — not mid-ocean ridges.

passages.title: Passage 4 — The Discovery of Penicillin
passages.text:
The discovery of penicillin in 1928 by the Scottish bacteriologist Alexander Fleming is one of the most celebrated stories in the history of medicine, often cited as an example of how chance and careful observation can combine to transform human health. Yet the path from accidental observation to life-saving drug was anything but simple, requiring more than a decade of additional research before penicillin became available to patients.

Fleming had been studying staphylococci, a group of bacteria that cause infections in humans, at St. Mary's Hospital in London. One morning in September 1928, after returning from a vacation, he noticed that a petri dish he had left out by mistake had become contaminated with a mold. Around the mold colony, the staphylococci had been destroyed, while bacteria elsewhere in the dish continued to grow normally. Recognizing that the mold appeared to produce a substance lethal to bacteria, Fleming isolated the mold and identified it as belonging to the genus Penicillium. He named the antibacterial substance penicillin.

Despite this remarkable observation, Fleming was unable to convert his discovery into a usable medicine. Penicillin proved difficult to purify and unstable when stored, and he eventually moved on to other projects. For more than a decade, penicillin remained little more than a laboratory curiosity.

It was a team at the University of Oxford, led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, that eventually transformed penicillin into a practical drug. Beginning in the late 1930s, they developed techniques to purify and concentrate the substance. By 1941, the team had administered penicillin to its first human patient. The results were astonishing: deadly infections that had previously been untreatable began to clear up within days.

The demands of World War II accelerated development. With wounded soldiers desperately in need of effective treatment for bacterial infections, the Allied governments invested heavily in mass production. By the end of the war, penicillin was being manufactured at an industrial scale, and it became widely available to civilian patients shortly afterward. Fleming, Florey, and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1945, recognizing their collective role in one of the greatest medical advances of the twentieth century.

options: A. Fleming alone is responsible for the success of penicillin.
B. The development of penicillin required both accidental discovery and years of further work.

questions.explanation: The passage traces how Fleming's chance observation was followed by years of work to make penicillin a usable medicine.

B. Bacteria destroyed around a mold colony.

questions.explanation: Fleming observed that staphylococci had been destroyed in the area around a mold colony.

questions.explanation: The passage credits the Oxford team led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain with developing penicillin into a practical drug.

questions.explanation: 'Astonishing' means remarkable or amazing.

questions.explanation: The passage states the Oxford team administered penicillin to its first human patient in 1941.

passages.title: Passage 5 — Indonesian Rainforest Biodiversity
passages.text:
Indonesia is home to one of the most biologically diverse rainforest systems on Earth, second only to the Amazon in total species richness. Stretching across the islands of Sumatra, Kalimantan (Borneo), Sulawesi, and Papua, these forests cover roughly half the country's land area and harbor species found nowhere else in the world. The biodiversity of Indonesian rainforests is the product of millions of years of geological isolation, climatic stability, and complex interactions between species.

One reason for this exceptional richness lies in the country's location at the meeting point of two biogeographical regions. The western islands, including Sumatra and Java, share many species with mainland Asia, while the eastern islands, particularly Papua, share species with Australia. The boundary between these regions runs through Indonesia and is known as the Wallace Line, named after the nineteenth-century naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace. Wallace observed that the fauna on one side of the line was strikingly different from that on the other — a discovery that helped lay the foundation for the field of biogeography.

Indonesian rainforests contain an extraordinary number of endemic species — that is, species found nowhere else. Sumatra and Borneo are home to orangutans, the only great apes native to Asia, while Java and Sumatra still shelter small populations of one-horned and two-horned rhinoceroses. The forests also support tigers, sun bears, clouded leopards, and thousands of bird species, including dozens of hornbill varieties. Plant diversity is no less impressive: a single hectare of Indonesian rainforest can contain more tree species than all of North America combined.

Despite this richness, Indonesian rainforests face severe threats. Logging — both legal and illegal — has reduced forest cover at an alarming rate. Conversion of forest to oil palm and pulpwood plantations is another major driver of deforestation. Fires, often set deliberately to clear land, have repeatedly produced massive smoke pollution that affects neighboring countries. Climate change adds further stress by altering rainfall patterns and increasing the risk of prolonged drought.

Conservation efforts include the establishment of protected areas such as Gunung Leuser, Tanjung Puting, and Lorentz National Parks, as well as international agreements aimed at curbing illegal timber trade. Some communities have also pioneered ecotourism and forest-friendly agriculture that allow local people to benefit economically without destroying habitat. Whether these efforts can preserve the rainforests' biodiversity in the long term will depend on sustained commitment from governments, businesses, and local people alike.

questions.question: What is the main topic of the passage?
options: A. The geography of Southeast Asia.
B. The biodiversity, importance, and threats facing Indonesian rainforests.
C. The career of Alfred Russel Wallace.
D. Methods for growing oil palm sustainably.
questions.explanation: The passage discusses Indonesian rainforest biodiversity, its origins, and the threats and conservation efforts surrounding it.

questions.question: According to the passage, why are Indonesian rainforests so biodiverse?
options: A. Because of recent volcanic activity.
B. Because of geological isolation, climatic stability, and species interactions over millions of years.

D. Because they have been protected from human impact.

questions.question: What is the Wallace Line?
options: A. A geological fault running through Indonesia.
B. A biogeographical boundary separating Asian and Australian species.
questions.explanation: The passage describes the Wallace Line as a biogeographical boundary running through Indonesia between Asian and Australian fauna.

questions.question: The word 'endemic' in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to:
options: B. found only in a specific place
questions.explanation: Endemic species are those found nowhere else, as the passage explicitly defines.

questions.question: Where are orangutans native?
options: B. Only in Sumatra and Borneo.
questions.explanation: The passage states orangutans are native to Sumatra and Borneo and are the only great apes native to Asia.

questions.question: What is one reason cited for high plant diversity in Indonesian rainforests?
options: A. A single hectare contains more tree species than all of North America combined.
B. They contain mainly imported plant species.
C. They are protected by international laws.
D. They grow on volcanic soils only.
questions.explanation: The passage offers this striking comparison to emphasize tree diversity in Indonesian rainforests.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a threat to the rainforests?
questions.explanation: The passage lists logging, plantations, fires, and climate change as threats — but not earthquakes.

questions.question: The word 'curbing' in paragraph 5 is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: 'Curbing' the illegal timber trade means limiting or restricting it.

questions.question: What conservation strategies does the passage mention?
options: B. Establishing protected areas, international agreements, ecotourism, and forest-friendly agriculture.
questions.explanation: The passage lists protected areas, international agreements, ecotourism, and forest-friendly farming as conservation approaches.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about the future of Indonesian rainforests?
options: A. They will be completely destroyed within a decade.
B. Their preservation depends on sustained commitment from multiple stakeholders.
C. They will recover automatically without intervention.
D. They are no longer biologically important.
questions.explanation: The final sentence emphasizes that preservation requires sustained commitment from governments, businesses, and local people.
